per_query.query: Seeing a spike in failed lookups from our DNS resolvers, roughly 12% above normal, with clients getting error responses instead of answers. Started around 07:00 UTC and lasted about four hours, concentrated in a few large data centers. Anyone else seeing this?
per_query.likely_cause: Based only on excerpt 12, a routine update to a major public resolver aimed at reducing memory usage changed the order of records in DNS responses. Some DNS client implementations expect CNAME records to appear before other records, so when the order shifted, their resolution began failing. The excerpt describes a January 8, 2026 incident affecting users across the Internet, which may or may not match the user's incident (07:00 UTC start, about four hours, concentrated in a few large data centers). The excerpt does not confirm that the user's resolvers run the same code or that this is the cause of their spike. It also does not give the user's own resolver configuration, dates, or failure-rate data, so the match is only partial.
per_query.suggested_fix: Check whether a recent change to your resolver software or its configuration altered the order of records in DNS responses, especially any memory-reduction or response-handling change, and roll it back if so. Compare your failing responses against the pre-change order to confirm the CNAME-ordering pattern. Identify which client implementations are failing and whether they assume CNAME-first ordering. The excerpt does not provide a specific remediation, so these steps are inferred and not documented in the excerpt. Also confirm that the upstream resolver incident in excerpt 12 is the same event before applying its remedy.

per_query.query: All scoreboards and their associated data disappeared at once, and the site was put into maintenance mode while we tried to recover. After coming back online, roughly seven hours of newly created scoreboards and added scores were permanently missing.
per_query.likely_cause: A database-reset function (one that drops the local database and recreates all tables from scratch) connected to the production database instead of a local one and wiped it. The excerpts say the team had not yet determined why the function targeted production. The data loss window was roughly 7 hours because the restore used the most recent daily managed-database backup, which predated the later scoreboards and scores. The excerpts do not explain why the connection pointed at production, so this part of the cause is only partly covered.
per_query.suggested_fix: Stop destructive reset/migration functions from running against production: separate production and local database credentials and hostnames, require explicit confirmation or an environment guard before any drop/recreate operation, and avoid running such code from a production-connected environment. For recovery, rely on backups with frequent point-in-time recovery or more frequent snapshots so the data-loss window is much smaller than one day. The excerpts do not cover the specific configuration error that caused the connection to production, so that root cause still needs to be confirmed.

per_query.query: Seeing widespread DNS resolution failures where lookups return empty answers for names that should resolve fine; some clients on Linux fail while others work. Started gradually over the last day and still ongoing. Anyone seen similar?
per_query.likely_cause: Most likely a DNS response record-ordering change in the resolver path. Excerpt 12 describes a case where a routine resolver update changed the order of records in DNS responses (CNAME placement), and some client implementations expect CNAME records before other records, so they fail to resolve names and return empty answers. The "some Linux clients fail, others work" pattern fits clients whose resolver libraries are sensitive to this ordering. Excerpt 1 is a different incident (a systemd patch breaking DNS on Ubuntu hosts) and only shows that a Linux client-side change can break resolution; it does not establish the cause here. The excerpts do not confirm which resolver or software update is involved in this incident, so this is a partial match based on the symptoms.
per_query.suggested_fix: Check whether a recent resolver or DNS software update changed response ordering, and compare responses from the failing and working resolvers (for example, dig the same name and inspect answer-section order). If a recent change is confirmed, roll back that update on the affected resolvers as a mitigation. For Linux hosts, check whether a recent systemd or resolver library patch was applied (as in excerpt 1) and roll back or pin the previous version on affected machines. Confirm the fix by re-running lookups on failing clients.

per_query.likely_cause: The incident appears to be two related problems. The exception processing delays match doc 87: datacenter maintenance caused network partitions in the cluster, delaying exception processing by up to 6-7 hours for some events, while the site stayed up and no exceptions were dropped. The account and billing write outage is only partly covered. Doc 130 describes a billing incident in which a redis-master cluster was lost or misconfigured, leaving balance data unavailable and blocking balance updates. The excerpts do not directly confirm that the same redis-master failure caused the current write outage. They also do not describe the current signup and password-change failures, so that link is an inference.
per_query.suggested_fix: For the processing delays: restore cluster connectivity after the network partitions and verify that queued exception processing drains. Review the network and datacenter maintenance procedure to prevent partitions. For the account and billing write outage: check the redis-master configuration and restore the store, preferably by promoting a slave rather than restarting redis-master, as doc 130 recommends. Restore billing balances from the independent double-bookkeeping datastore if balance data was lost. Until balances can be written, add fail-safes so that accounts are not suspended and cards are not charged when balance data is missing or unwritable. The excerpts do not give a complete step-by-step runbook, so verify each step against the live system.

per_query.query: Seeing error pages instead of content for requests through our edge network, and in a separate case blank pages returned to users. Both events hit a large share of traffic globally and cleared up on their own within roughly half an hour to a couple of hours.
per_query.likely_cause: The excerpts describe a Cloudflare-style edge incident (Nov 18, 2025) in which a bad configuration (feature) file was generated and propagated to the network, causing fluctuating good/bad config distribution and 5xx error pages across core CDN services; the bad file originated from ClickHouse nodes generating it. This matches the error-page symptom and its fluctuating, self-recovering pattern, though the excerpts do not explicitly describe the blank-page event. A separate excerpt (Oct 25, 2022) describes a CDN software release bug causing HTTP 530 errors for customers using Tiered Cache, Images, or Bandwidth Alliance, which may relate to the error-page symptom but does not explain blank pages. The excerpts only partly cover the incident: the blank-page cause is not identified.
per_query.suggested_fix: For the config-driven error pages: stop generation and propagation of the bad configuration file, restore a known-good file into the distribution queue, and force a restart of the core proxy; then restart any services left in a bad state. Add validation of generated configuration files before propagation and staged rollout of config changes. For the 530 pattern: roll back the faulty CDN component release and use staged rollout. The blank-page event needs further investigation, as the excerpts do not cover its cause.
